I have been wrong countless times with short-term expectations, so I'm not trying to take my own victory lap regarding the commodity's trajectory. I'd suggest looking at the forward curve for the commodity, including the long-term contract terms currently being signed. posts.text:
Citi Research spoke with $NBIS management in a group callback after the Q3 2026 report and published its takeaways the same afternoon. T

The note is the clearest explanation so far of why Q4 came in light, how much cushion sits in the 2027 guide and how next year's build will be funded.

The ARR story:
The ARR miss is a matter of weeks. Without the Microsoft-related delays, the third-party colocation sites due in December would have taken ARR above $7bn. 

They slipped one to two months, which moves the milestone into the new year rather than removing it. This matches the shareholder letter's shift of the ~$7bn ARR target from December to February.

2027 Guidance:
Management calls the 2027 guide conservative. It is built to hold even if Nebius's own data centers are late by many months, so on-time delivery would be upside to the $12–13bn revenue outlook. 

The 800 MW–1 GW connected-power target was not repeated, and investors should assume Microsoft and other delays are factored in.

Financing:
The 2027 outlook assumes $17–20bn of customer prepayments, and a significant part of that is committed under existing contracts and paid before the capacity is delivered.

General:
Management sees third-party colocation partners as less reliable, sometimes one to two months late or more, which is why most 2027 data centers will be company-owned.

Owned sites help margins later. They put an appreciating asset on the balance sheet instead of a lease in the P&L. The full benefit appears only at scale, once Nebius is no longer bringing many sites online at once: from late 2027, and more clearly in 2028.

Token Factory is heading toward a multi-hundred-million-dollar ARR on signed contracts that expand as new capacity comes online, with more growth expected in Q1 and through 2027.

Customers can switch between the managed service and direct infrastructure, so management does not attribute revenue to one delivery method; that flexibility is a key reason customers choose Nebius. 

Management also expects inference on open-source models to keep growing fast.

Conclusion:
Citi derives its one-year target from a regression of software-company trading multiples against growth and profitability, projecting Nebius through FY2029. 

It then applies a 73% discount to the regression-implied multiple to reflect the financial leverage of future buildouts. The $265 target implies about 6x 2027 EV/revenue. 

Citi cut its target to $265 from $324 on November 3, before the Q3 report, and kept it after the callback.

I’m a Piece of Sh--’: Jensen Huang’s Last Hours as Nvidia CEO

Summary by Bloomberg AI
▪Jensen Huang's surrender to leave his job as Nvidia Corp.'s chief executive officer was unconditional after weeks of denying allegations of infidelity.
▪Huang had given up, according to a person familiar with the situation, and his usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated.
▪The board of directors announced that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO after Huang's resignation, and the company will now confront the challenge of finding a replacement for him.

By Drake Bennett and Ian King
11/12/2026 19:28:55 [BN]

(Bloomberg) -- At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying the allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia Corp.’s chief executive officer, his surrender late Wednesday night was unconditional. Huang’s usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he’d started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” 

For the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up. 

It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigor, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours. 

It’s hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and their chips, and it’s hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company’s board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang’s ouster, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.”

Huang couldn’t be reached for comment. 
￼
When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang’s, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them.

Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He’d been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said. 
￼
A turning point came last Friday, Nov. 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one.  Soon afterward, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang’s house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn’t want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The board announced that they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologizing to his family and vowing to “cooperate fully” with the board’s investigation.
￼
As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang’s attention away from his extensive duties at the company.

URANIUM: FUEL BUYERS ARE TURNING BULLISH WHILE WALL STREET SELLS

Mike Alkin of Sachem Cove joined Erik Townsend on MacroVoices (Nov. 12) to explain a strange split: uranium prices remain firm, but uranium equities are being sold alongside AI and data-center stocks.

Alkin says the bull market never needed AI. Roughly 440 operating reactors, plus a pipeline of 80 more, already require more economically viable uranium than mines can supply at current prices. He estimates structural deficits of 15–25% or more of demand, with nuclear growth accelerating from roughly 0.5% to 4–5% annually.

So why are uranium stocks trading like AI stocks?

Some junior miners marketed themselves as data-center beneficiaries. Banks included nuclear shares in AI and momentum baskets. Now fears of an AI spending bust trigger selling regardless of uranium fundamentals. Flows overwhelm facts.

Fuel buyers are moving the other way.

Alkin has attended Nuclear Energy Institute conferences since 2018, when buyers dismissed his shortage thesis. At the latest meeting, he said he could barely find a bearish fuel buyer willing to debate him. Yet utilities are contracting for only a little over half their annual requirements, leaning on older contracts and inventories.

They have barely tested the supply market. Alkin expects more than 2 billion pounds to require contracting through 2040. After roughly 15 years of inventory drawdowns, utilities may eventually have to buy more than they consume to rebuild stocks.

Long-term uranium prices have already roughly quadrupled despite weak contracting. Tenders that once attracted 7–12 bids now draw very few. Producers with limited capacity have little incentive to sell cheaply. Meanwhile, Alkin says about 70% of uranium is produced in the East while 70% is consumed in the West.

Mining costs are another part of the shortage.

He cited industry estimates of average uranium production costs rising from $24/lb in 2019 to $38/lb in 2025. Kazatomprom once projected costs near $13–14/lb for 2026; he puts them at $38–45/lb today, or above $55/lb using the old exchange rate. Across the industry, projects have suffered major overruns and production misses.

Small mines producing 0.5–2 million pounds a year are particularly exposed. Delayed production supports the uranium price but can destroy returns for shareholders in the companies that fail to deliver. Alkin argues proven operators deserve a scarcity premium.

He used Cameco as an example. Investors focused on its disappointing quarter, but Alkin highlighted something else: Cameco indicated it was signing contracts at triple-digit uranium prices, above the reported long-term benchmark around $98–99/lb. He estimates Cameco trades at about 8–9x EBITDA after valuing its Westinghouse stake, compared with roughly 31x in 2022. That estimate depends on his valuation assumptions.

Elsewhere in the fuel cycle, conversion pricing has risen from roughly $4 to over $60/kg and enrichment from around $30 to over $200/SWU, according to Alkin. His argument: uranium has not yet experienced the same buyer panic.

For investors, he drew a clear distinction. Physical uranium removes mine-level operating risk. Mining equities offer greater leverage to rising prices but carry serious execution risk. The Sprott Physical Uranium Trust was discussed at roughly an 18% discount to NAV, which can persist or widen.

Erik raised factory-built advanced reactors as a possible additional demand shock. Alkin agreed they could worsen shortages but said his thesis does not depend on them. He cited current contract floors near $70–75/lb and ceilings around $150–160/lb. A rush to secure supply could force a sharper price adjustment, but he gave no timetable.

The contrast: Wall Street is selling uranium miners over AI fears while the fuel buyers themselves are increasingly concerned about available supply.

The Cycle Isn’t Over. Demand for Intelligence Has No Human Ceiling

Every past tech cycle ended for the same reason: demand ran out of people. There were only so many households to buy a PC, so many users to get online and so many people to carry a smartphone. Once adoption saturated, capacity caught up, prices broke and the cycle turned.

AI breaks that pattern. Demand for intelligence isn’t capped by human headcount, because machines consume it too. AI agents call other agents, models generate their own training data, and reasoning models burn many times more tokens on every query. Each gain in efficiency becomes more consumption, not spare capacity.

The data shows it:

•  H100 rents are at a record: renting a previous-generation H100 now costs $3.10 an hour, up 56% in a year. In a normal cycle, legacy chips get cheaper as new chips arrive. Blackwell is shipping, yet the H100 still isn’t obsolete, and it’s earning more.

•  Usage is compounding: token volume is up about 40-fold in a year, even as the price per token fell from about $2.00 to $0.80.

•  Inventories are thin: memory makers hold under 10 days of supply.

A cycle ends when supply overtakes demand. Rising prices for old hardware tell you supply is still chasing demand. Wall st. can argue about multiples, but the earnings cycle isn’t over.

I believe Jensen’s resignation could have significant implications for memory companies, particularly their relationship with NVIDIA around NVHBM.

Of course, NVIDIA is unlikely to change its NVHBM roadmap immediately just because Jensen is gone. What I am watching is the influence that persuaded suppliers to commit to that roadmap. In my view, Jensen played a major role in laying out future demand, convincing suppliers to invest ahead of it, and securing favorable pricing and supply allocations. My biggest question is whether his successor can maintain the same level of trust and influence under these circumstances.

Take SK hynix, for example. According to industry research, SK hynix reportedly supplies NVIDIA with HBM at lower prices than it charges NVIDIA’s competitors, even for the same performance bin. Accepting a somewhat lower price still made sense in exchange for substantial volume and long term business opportunities. I believe that relationship also helped SK hynix navigate the recent HBM4 situation.

But what if Jensen’s absence creates more uncertainty around NVIDIA’s execution and growth prospects, while incremental demand shifts toward Google’s and OpenAI’s custom chips or AMD? And what if that demand keeps growing? If memory suppliers can secure sufficient volume and better terms from other customers, wouldn’t they have less reason to offer NVIDIA especially favorable pricing or prioritize it when allocating limited engineering resources and production capacity?

Looking at NVHBM through that lens, I think we could see changes ahead. Consider Samsung. It had to accept what could arguably be seen as a humiliating requirement to use base dies manufactured by TSMC for NVHBM. But if overall AI demand holds up while its customer base diversifies, might Samsung have room to make a different choice?

Of course, none of this is certain, and it remains speculation. Still, I think these potential shifts in the memory industry are worth watching closely. I will continue tracking developments and sharing my insights.

posts.text:
Yesterday @bhalligan said he and @dharmesh are refounding HubSpot as the "Customer Harness Company"

That sounds right to me and it's super exciting! 

But what does it mean? I think right now at least, we'll all have different takes. We are all at different stages of our agent journeys, in general and in GTM specifically. 

Here's what it means for us, at least right now, November 2026 :)

#1. We are 100% headless on our CRM and never going back

No one logs into CRM on our human team anymore. And 10K, our AI VP Revenue, and our other agents MCP/API in.

We will never log into B2B software again.  

#2.  We don't need traditional marketing automation anymore. That's dead. But we need  agentic marketing

Over the last 60 days we've moved off traditional marketing automation entirely. We still to do marketing.  Our list is 450k+, and we send millions of emails and more.  But it's now done almost entirely agentically.

We don't need templates for emails and promos. 10K has built all those, and we rebuild them dynamically for each send in a way no template ever could. In fact, many of our emails are 100% personalized for real to each recipient, even at mass scale.

And yes, consent is incredibly important, as is deliverability. But you can get that headless from many top tier vendors here. This doesn't lock you in anymore.

We will never buy marketing automation software every again. It was for humans. 

#3. Claude + Chat GPT and Slack are great, but who knows if that's the killer interface

I just don't know. For us, running this inside our agents is still easier, and using the custom interface in the agents. Especially since its multiplayer.  Running your GTM inside of Claude and ChatGPT or Slack are a great surface, but for us at least, they aren't going to be the primary surface.

For us, we just talk to 10K like a human. That works best. Like a human that never stops working, and makes plenty of mistakes.  But it has all our context, all our history, all our data from multiple sources (including Quickbooks, Bill, etc). So it's our best 'surface'.  Not Claude or ChatGPT.  

#4.  We use the best agent for the job, period. We and 10K do not really care if it comes from our CRM or other 'core' providers. At all

This may change. And it's all in flux. But honestly, we don't care if our CRM and other apps have agents if they aren't the right tool for the job. We pick best-of-breed, at least for the moment, see if we can deploy it very quickly, test if for real (evals), and then ... Go.  

#5. There is no agent loyalty but it is hard to get us to look at other agents once we're 'happy'

There is a real urgency here, and it's why the timing is right for HubSpot. All of us were loyal for years to our favorite classic B2B vendors, Salesforce shops, HubSpot shops, Shopify shops.  In many ways, we still are.

But our agents aren't. They do pick favorites, and they do pick leaders. But they are not remotely loyal.

We had a core vendor go down for 48 hours. We were loyal. 10K wasn't. He routed around it. 

And we never went back.

I joined @CNBC's The Exchange to discuss what I've been calling Schrödinger's Strait: a Strait that is neither fully open nor fully closed. 

We know that barrels are getting through, keeping the prompt oil market relatively in balance and maintaining prices in the $85–$100 range - but it does nothing to make the next one cheaper.

We need to look beyond whether or not the barrels are passing through the Strait and assess the real issue, which is the extraordinary cost of delivering oil to consumers - a bubbling cauldron of supply and demand  imbalances - shipping, insurance, refining, logistics, any one of which can become the next problem and all of which are combining to ensure the price of delivered barrel of oil is as high as it has been through this entire episode.

That's why I think the war trade in prompt oil has largely played out, but the regime trade remains very much intact. 

The market is relatively balanced today, the front-end is relatively flat and tame. But the structural cost of securing future supply hasn't gone away. My longer-term focus remains on long-dated oil, drillers and producers.

엔비디아를 제외한 고객사중에는 27년 HBM4로 바로 전환하기보다 HBM3E로 용량과 대역폭을 확대하다가 28년 HBM4를 도입하거나 바로 HBM4E로 점프하는 움직임도 꽤 보임. 앤스로픽은 대놓고 이러한 전략을 공개함.

핵심은 HBM4의 수익성과 범용 DRAM의 공급 부족임.

범용 DRAM 수급이 안정되려면 웨이퍼당 Bit 생산량이 20% 이상 증가하는 D1c 공정 물량이 시장에 유의미하게 공급돼야 하는데, 아무리 빨라도 2027년 중순 이후로 예상됨.

문제는 그때까지 HBM4의 수익성이 범용 DRAM대비 심각할정도로 낮다는것. 실제로 이번 하이닉스와 삼성 영업이익 차이가 많이 좁혀졌는데 삼성이 CAPA 증가물량을 죄다 HBM4에 쏟아부은 영향이라는 얘기도 있음.

HBM은 DRAM 노드가 미세화되더라도 웨이퍼당 실질 Bit 생산량 증가가 매우 적음. 결국 범용 DRAM 대비 낮아지는 생산성을 가격 인상으로 보전해야 하는데, 동일한 이익률을 확보하려면 고객사가 받아들이기 어려운 가격이 형성될 수밖에 없음. 게다가 현재 하닉마이크론은 HBM4 Bit 공급 가능량이 시장 기대치보다 훨씬 낮음.

고객사 입장에서도 HBM4의 가격 부담도  상당하고 공급량도 적기때문에 당장은 HBM3E를 연장하고 2028년 HBM4E 도입 시점에 범용 DRAM 가격 안정화와 함께 가격 협상에 나서는 편이 유리할수도 있음. 추론 서비스 제공자들의 현재 병목은 대역폭보다는 서비스 확대를 위한 DRAM 절대용량이 더 큰 상황이라 무리하게 당장 HBM4로 전환하는건 쉽지 않아보임.

제조사 역시 무리하게 HBM4 공급을 확대하기보다 적정 점유율을 유지하면서 수익성이 높은 범용 DRAM 생산에 더욱 집중할것으로 보임. 

결국 2027년 HBM 공급 부족은 심각할거 같고, HBM3E의 수명은 예상보다 길어질거라고 봄.

Three signs the tide is turning our way

A month ago, India was the market nobody wanted to touch. Today, looks like FIIs can’t get back in fast enough. Funny how quickly the story changes.

We are seeing a possible regime shift over the last week or two. The narrative for FIIs seems to have flipped from ‘Anywhere but India’ to ‘India, the safe haven’. Too early to say if it sustains, but it is a welcome change.

Let me walk you through three signs that the tide may finally be turning our way, and one global risk staring at all of us.

One: The FIIs are coming back

₹60,698 Cr. That is what FPIs have bought in Indian equities in just seven trading days of November. The highest net buying over any seven consecutive trading days since January 2021.

Two: The earnings are strong

Q2 is almost done, and it turned out far better than anyone expected. Remember the backdrop we walked into Q2 with, crude above $100, geopolitical tension, sea routes and logistics disrupted. And still, India Inc delivered.

The median revenue growth for Nifty 50 and NSE 500 stands at 17.4% and 18.6%. Median PAT at 22.3% and 20.4%, as of Nov 10th. Numbers like these, in a quarter like that, tell you something about the quality of these businesses.

Three: The valuations are right

The market went nowhere while earnings kept doing their job, and the result is a market that looks reasonable even after this run-up. Nifty 50 is at a one-year forward PE of around 18x (5Y median 20.8x), Nifty Midcap 150 around 25x (5Y median 30x), Nifty Smallcap 250 at 29x (5Y median 28.3x). 

Broadly, nothing stretched. There is no euphoria out there. If anything, there is still a fair bit of despair.

Coming to our Surge India performance:

Surge India was down -4.1% in Oct 2026, as compared to our primary benchmark Nifty 50 TRI at +1.9% and secondary benchmark Nifty 500 Multicap 50:25:25 TRI at -1.8%.

Surge delivered a strong Q2. The median revenue growth is at 34% YoY, and median PAT growth is at 50.4% (as of Nov 10th).

Our top 3 sectors continue to be Automobiles & Components (21.7%), Capital Goods (20.5%) and Pharmaceuticals (19.7%), and we remain bullish on all three.

To summarise,

After two years of waiting, three things have finally turned our way at the same time, the liquidity is coming back, earnings are strong, and the valuations are still sane. None of them alone means much. Together, they are the best setup we have seen in two years.

Yes, there is a global risk flashing in the background, and we are watching it closely. But you never get a clean setup with zero risk; those don’t exist. You get moments where the odds quietly turn in your favour, and this feels like one of them.

全世界都在吃黄仁勋的瓜，却没几个人注意他临走前留下的那张 5300 亿美元的账单。

由于被董事会调查与多名下属的不当关系，外加与一名被怀疑替北京效力的客户有染，干了 33 年的黄仁勋突然辞去CEO，由首席财务官 Colette Kress 临时接替。

人虽然走了，但他用英伟达资产负债表给整个 AI 行业搭起来的巨大杠杆，还悬在半空。

翻开英伟达最新的二季度 10-Q 财报，它披露的表外义务总额已经从上季度的 1840 亿美元猛增到了 5300 亿美元。

这 5300 亿美元里，包含了从 1190 亿飙到 2790 亿美元的供应与产能承诺，大头是黄仁勋在 2025 年趁别人还没反应过来、亲自飞去韩国锁死的内存产能。靠着他跟供应商老板一对一的交情，以及优先给 SK 集团分配显卡的默契，英伟达拿到的 2027 年 HBM4 内存价格预计只有每 Gb 3.0 到 3.3 美元，而 AMD、博通、亚马逊和谷歌去买就得掏 3.7 到 4.1 美元。

如果说上游是卡脖子，那下游就是赤裸裸的“英伟达央行”了。

表外账单里另外几块暴涨的科目，全是替客户背的雷：帮 OpenAI 租下俄亥俄州园区做的土地和电力外壳担保，从 35 亿直接跳到了 1085 亿美元；另外还新冒出了 360 亿美元的“新云”收入包销保底协议，以及 200 亿美元的数据中心租约。至于账上，它手里还攥着 990 亿美元的股权投资。

市面上那些连投资级信用评级都没有的“新云”厂商和初创实验室，为什么能绕开传统云巨头借到便宜钱？很大程度上就是因为黄仁勋在给他们作保。英伟达第一天按全额利润把显卡卖给他们，转头就给买家的云收入保底、替买家向房东担保，甚至自己直接出面把租约签下来。

这套靠“黄仁勋看跌期权”运转的生态，很大程度上押在他一个人的威望和胆魄上。

当然，算力需求本身不假。而且据报道英伟达在 9 月份就已经暂停了新的“新云”保底交易。

但麻烦在于，英伟达过去 33 年从来就是围绕黄仁勋一个人建起来的，高管们平时连抛头露面都被刻意压制，所有重大决策全由他一人拍板。接下来无论是呼声最高的 CUDA 之父 Ian Buck 还是 Jonah Alben 接任正式 CEO，一个职业经理人当家的英伟达，大概率会像乔布斯走后的苹果一样变得保守，把大把现金拿去股票回购，而不是继续替客户签字画押。

要知道，英伟达的芯片现在虽然紧俏，但要想守住高昂的溢价，就得继续拿托底承诺撑着新云厂商；一旦新 CEO 对支持新云稍有犹豫，GPU 现货租价就可能下跌，利润被压扁的新云只好掉头去找 AMD 或谷歌 TPU 阵营。

新云一走，英伟达的订单量跟着缩水，它靠大订单锁死上游供应链的飞轮可能也就此断掉。

这个靠教父个人信用撑起来的算力生态很可能会迎来一轮大幅收缩，而上游供应链预计到 2028 年也会有超过七成的产能流向非英伟达客户。那个敢拿公司身家替全行业兜底的狂飙时代，恐怕也要跟着翻篇了。

🚨 輝達（NVIDIA）又爆出一個大雷，這次跟老黃的婚外情半毛錢關係都沒有。

《華爾街日報》剛把底牌全掀了：買不起晶片？輝達直接掏出幾百億美元做財務擔保，硬幫 AI 公司把單子簽下來。

在公司裡推這套玩法的，就是老黃自己的女婿 Nico Caprez。他今年 1 月剛升上副總裁，手下團隊直接對外放話，跟那些小型雲端廠和數據中心建商說：只要兩週，輝達就能幫你們把信貸支持搞定。

目的就一個：把這幫人死死綁成輝達 GPU 的長期買家。

這套操作把表外承諾的盤子吹到了天上。輝達最新財報白紙黑字寫著，各類承諾與擔保總額直接飆到 5,300 億美元——就在一個季度前，這個數字還只有 1,840 億美元。

公司內部其實有人踩煞車，CFO Colette Kress 當時就一直提出質疑，反覆追問這些擔保到底怎麼定價、輝達真正能拿回什麼。

結果今年 8 月開會時，老黃直接打斷她的話，當眾罵她「像隻被車頭燈照傻的鹿（a deer in the headlights）」。

儘管被老闆當眾洗臉，Kress 還是硬把輝達對 OpenAI 俄亥俄州數據中心的擔保額度，從 2,500 億美元砍到了 1,050 億美元。

現在風水輪流轉，老黃走人了，當年被罵的那個 CFO 坐上了臨時 CEO 的位子。

要看懂這顆雷有多大，先看懂這套「AI 資金閉環」是怎麼轉的：   

輝達投錢給 AI 公司，或者幫它的貸款和租賃做擔保。   
這家公司拿著這筆錢和信用去蓋數據中心。  

數據中心裡塞滿輝達的 GPU。   輝達把這批 GPU 算進自己的銷售營收。   

萬一這家公司算力租不出去，輝達還承諾把沒用完的算力買回來。

看明白了嗎？同一筆交易裡，輝達同時當投資人、放款人、供應商，外加接盤俠。錢從輝達口袋掏出去，轉一圈又變成了輝達的營收。

CoreWeave 就是最現成的例子。輝達既持有它的股份、賣晶片給它，還簽約承諾在 2032 年前買下它最多 63 億美元的閒置算力。

盤子最大的是 OpenAI。輝達給它俄亥俄州數據中心提供高達 1,050 億美元的擔保、包辦裡面所有晶片，還順手往承建這座數據中心的公司投了 15 億美元。

翻開輝達截至 7 月 26 日那一季的財報，錢全卡在這些地方：

記憶體與晶圓採購承諾：2,790 億美元（前一季才 1,190 億美元）

OpenAI 俄亥俄州數據中心擔保：最高 1,050 億美元

向新興雲端廠（neoclouds）回購閒置算力的協議：360 億美元

再看一眼資產負債表上的實際負債：910 億美元。

也就是說，輝達表外的承諾金額，差不多是帳面債務的 6 倍。

只要市場不出事，輝達確實不會虧這筆錢，畢竟擔保只有在客戶違約付不出錢時才會觸發。

但現在問題來了，連老黃自己之前都開始慌了。《華爾街日報》披露，老黃曾私下警告高管，幾家大型雲端巨頭正在加速轉向自研晶片，想擺脫對輝達的依賴。與此同時，輝達自己簽約鎖死的晶圓和記憶體，正像「雪崩」一樣排山倒海壓過來。

大客戶想跑路，上游供應鏈合約又死死鎖著不能退，底下全靠輝達拿信用在幫小客戶續命。

posts.text:
This is absolutely brilliant, by legendary Australian investor John Hempton, who explains the core financial paradox at the heart of the AI story (and which also, to some extent, may explain the Jensen Huang story).

The numbers say that about $7 trillion in AI compute is set to be built by 2030. For the industry to earn that back, given those chips have a roughly 5-year lifespan and cost a lot to run, they need to generate about $2 trillion of AI revenue a year.

Hempton says the only way you can get to these sorts of numbers is by selling AI as a productivity tool to businesses, meaning replacing workers.

And since, for reasons he explains in the video, no company fires people to save just 10% in costs, the savings have to be about double what businesses pay for the AI: roughly $4 trillion in savings on wages a year.

What does firing $4 trillion worth of workers mean concretely? Hempton calculated this equates to roughly 10% of the OECD’s total wage bill of about $40 trillion: one in every ten dollars paid to workers across the OECD’s 38 member countries.

Which, naturally, when you suddenly take that much income out of people’s pockets, would trigger a massive global recession.

And here's the paradox: in a massive global recession, there's no way businesses will pay $2 trillion a year for AI, so the return disappears anyway.

In other words, AI's only possible path to success given the numbers requires destroying the very economy that is supposed to pay for it.

HOWEVER - and here's where the Nvidia/Jensen Huang story might come into play (and, to be clear, this is now me speaking and not Hempton given this interview is prior to the whole Nvidia saga) - this all rests on a core assumption: that compute stays super expensive. Which in practice means Nvidia keeping its pricing power, with a 75% gross margin on its chips. 

Break Nvidia's pricing power, and the $7 trillion bill, the $2 trillion in revenue and the 10% of jobs all shrink with it.

This would also put the whole China story in a different light. Maybe it's not so much a "we don't want the Chinese to be competitive with similar chips to us" story as it is a "we don't want Chinese demand to drive up chip prices" one. Or probably both.

And, as such, you could actually think about the US export controls not as a national security measure but as a good old subsidy for US AI players (together with a handicap for their Chinese competitors), a way to limit the price of chips. 

This holds even with China itself blocking Nvidia imports, since Chinese firms simply rent the chips abroad instead, in places like Southeast Asia, which is precisely what this whole Alice Huang/Megaspeed story is about.

The main obstacle for all this was, of course... Jensen. Obviously, the guy wanted the exact opposite: as many buyers as possible, Chinese players included, to keep chip prices and Nvidia’s margins sky-high. He was also the one man with the clout to make that happen.

All hard to prove, of course, but I can imagine that quite a few corks popped this week in Anthropic's offices: nothing like the news that the man keeping your biggest cost sky-high is out when you're a week away from a $1.2 trillion IPO.

At a separate event on Tuesday evening, Bowman was asked by the Heritage Foundation's E.J. Antoni about how monetary policy could be effective at dealing with today's inflation if it is being driven by an energy supply shock.

***

ANTONI: So looking at the inflation that we see today, I think it's pretty clear if you look at not just the headline CPI numbers, but then you look at the core numbers, you look at trimmed mean and median, that what we're dealing with is primarily, if not exclusively, an energy shock. And in fact, we saw in those different ways that you can remove out buyers from the index, the inflation readings were continuing to fall until September, and now it's really just the last couple of months that we are seeing energy inflation, if you will, kind of spill out of the gas tank and hit everything else in the broader economy. 

So how does the Fed navigate something like an energy shock that we have today where the problem is not actually a monetary phenomenon, but instead the problem is really a supply shock? And if that's the case, how does that, if at all, change the way you and the Fed more broadly look at how they can use monetary tools to address what looks like a non-monetary problem? 

BOWMAN: EJ, that's a great question. And I address that in my remarks as well because generally with an energy shock, you try to look through that for as long as you can. But because we've been experiencing it for as long as we have, it is, I think over the last few inflation reports, we've seen that the inflation pressures have been broadening. And so we've reached the point where I don't think that you can as obviously look through them, especially as we have a strong labor market and we have a dual mandate, full employment and stable prices. So I think especially with today's CPI print, it just indicates to me that the time has come, for me anyway, to shift the focus to inflation and trying to lower inflation.

October PPI: Wholesale Inflation Implies Rising PPE and December Fed Rate Hike

Wholesale inflation advanced 0.3% in both the headline and core in October, which resulted in a 6.5% increase in the former and a 5% increase in the latter. The September estimate saw an upward revision to 1.4% from 1.3% in the headline number and to 0.8% from 0.7%.

Inflation is broadening as topline increases bleed into the core with a 3-to-4-month lag which has resulted in sharply rising transportation and food costs.

Data from both the CPI and PPI used to estimate the PCE that the Fed utilizes to make policy point towards a 3.8% increase in inflation over the past year and a 3.2% advance in the core. While the November data will look much better due to the recent ease in oil and energy costs it will not provide sufficient relief to policymakers to avoid a December rate hike.

We think that the PPI data and the forward look on the PCE locks in a twenty-five-basis point Fed rate hike as the central bank has fallen behind the curve on inflation.

Supertanker Squeeze Crimping US Oil Exports, Texas Port CEO Says

A shortage of available oil supertankers is constraining US crude exports, prompting shippers to hire smaller vessels and direct more cargoes to Europe, according to the head of the largest US port.

For the first time in four years, not a single very large crude carrier, or VLCC, entered the US Gulf of Mexico to collect an oil cargo last week, Port of Corpus Christi Chief Executive Officer Kent Britton said in an interview with Bloomberg News on Thursday. 

At Corpus Christi’s port, oil-export terminals are relying on smaller vessels known as Suezmaxes and Aframaxes that are cheaper to hire than VLCCs, according to Britton. 

“They’re having to move twice as many ships to get the same amount of oil out, it’s just creating a little bit of a bottleneck at the dock,” he said. (Bloomberg)
